item.title: Kagoshima Events 2026: Kinko Bay Fireworks, Ohara Matsuri & Sakurajima
item.description: Kagoshima lives in the shadow of Sakurajima, one of the world’s most active volcanoes, which smokes across the bay from the city every day. Its 2026 event calendar matches that drama: Kyushu’s largest fireworks display over Kinko Bay, southern Japan’s biggest street dance festival, and the year-round spectacle of the volcano itself. Add the steaming sand baths of Ibusuki and the ancient forests of Yakushima offshore, and Kagoshima rewards a well-timed 2026 trip.

item.title: Sakurajima & Osumi Cycling — Guide
item.description: Cycling is a wonderful way to experience the dramatic scenery around Sakurajima and the Osumi Peninsula in Kagoshima. Sakurajima island itself has a roughly 36 km road looping most of the way around it, and cycling here takes you past solidified lava fields, seaside footbaths, observation points with close-up volcano views, small villages and fertile fields of volcanic-soil produce, with the smoking cone as a constant backdrop. Rental bikes, including e-bikes to help with the hills, are available near the ferry terminal.

item.title: Sakurajima Lava Nagisa Footbath — Guide
item.description: The Sakurajima Nagisa Lava Footbath (Nagisa Yumeguri Onsen) is a delightful and completely free attraction on the shore of Sakurajima island, and a lovely way to relax while taking in the volcano. Stretching about 100 metres along the coast, it is one of the longest footbaths in Japan. Set among the black solidified lava rocks of the shoreline, the footbath is fed by natural hot-spring water heated by the volcano’s geothermal energy, and as you sit and soak your tired feet in the warm water, you enjoy open views across Kinko Bay back toward Kagoshima city, with the great cone of Sakurajima rising behind you.

item.title: Sakurajima Volcano — Guide
item.description: Sakurajima is one of the world’s most active volcanoes and the iconic symbol of Kagoshima, looming dramatically across Kinko Bay from the city. This towering volcanic peak erupts frequently — sometimes puffing plumes of ash over the city daily — and a lava flow in 1914 was so vast it joined the former island to the Osumi Peninsula. Despite its fury, people live on its slopes, and it’s easily and safely visited by a short, scenic ferry from Kagoshima city (running 24 hours).

item.title: Osaka Bay Guide: Kaiyukan, the Ferris Wheel & Sakurajima
item.description: West of the city centre, Osaka Bay opens the metropolis to the sea — a breezy waterfront of attractions, harbour views, and big-sky sunsets that makes a refreshing change from the neon canyons of Minami. Here you’ll find the giant Tempozan Ferris wheel, the superb Kaiyukan aquarium, sightseeing cruises, and, across the water on Sakurajima, Universal Studios Japan. It’s family territory and a great spot to watch the sun sink over the harbour.

item.title: Best Hotels & Ryokan in Kagoshima: Ibusuki, Kirishima & Sakurajima
item.description: Kagoshima Prefecture — Japan’s volcanic southern gateway — sits at the tip of Kyushu with active volcanoes, subtropical islands, and some of Japan’s most distinctive onsen experiences. Ibusuki offers the world’s only natural sand bath (sunamushi) powered by geothermal heat, Kirishima provides highland volcanic resort scenery, and Sakurajima volcano dominates the entire region’s skyline. Best Areas to Stay Kagoshima City — Sakurajima Views The prefectural capital faces the active Sakurajima volcano across a narrow bay — ash occasionally falls on the city, which locals consider normal.
